THE SILENT CONVOY
By Marcus Chen

Autonomous vehicles were the backbone of modern military logistics—and particularly in modern naval convoy operations. If you could disrupt all autonomous navigation systems—silence of that sort would be deadly to any military force dependent on technological progress.

The urgent beeping of the proximity alarm jolted Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence from his review of the convoy routes. He rose from his station chair in the command center of the autonomous cargo vessel Meridian, stretching his tall frame and running a hand through his dark hair. That would be Ava Hernández, his systems engineer. Hernández always signaled that way—three short bursts, like someone who believed every situation was an emergency.

Lawrence didn't rush. It pleased him to let Hernández wait a moment. He moved deliberately to the door, paused there, and glanced back at the woman working intently at the design station—Dr. Jennifer Lambert, the elderly architect and systems designer, a civilian consultant for the United States Navy.

The weathered face of the older woman was set in concentrated lines, her silver hair pulled back as she bent over her holographic display. Lawrence caught a glimpse of the architectural design she was working on—some kind of modular port facility with distinctive coastal influences—and his lips relaxed slightly. The Navy had arranged for Lambert to continue her infrastructure work during the voyage, since their destination happened to align with her current project.

Lambert had joined them in Bridgewater, Selvoria two days before departure. With her came a shipment of experimental equipment, including several containers of what looked like advanced sensor arrays, now stored in the forward cargo bay. Lambert had supervised the loading with meticulous care, and spent hours daily in the converted storage room that served as her temporary design studio.

Sometimes, Lawrence thought Lambert was overly paranoid—an architect whose mind had been affected by the economic inequality she'd witnessed in the refugee camps of Riverside, Xandria, where her humanitarian work had taken her before this assignment. At other times, the woman seemed brilliant. Perhaps that was the answer—a brilliant mind scarred by what she'd seen.

Lawrence opened the door and looked out. Rain hammered against the observation deck like liquid bullets. Overhead, the sky was a storm-wracked mass of clouds, broken in one spot by a small patch of star-studded darkness.

His eyes rested on the face of the woman before him. It was Hernández, her dark brows drawn down over intense brown eyes; her angular face tight with tension; her hands gripping a data tablet. Rain streaked down her cheeks, leaving glistening trails.

The woman was a puzzle to Lawrence. She was inexplicably close to a problematic crew member named Robert Valdez—the most vocal critic of the autonomous systems on board. But there was no question of her technical ability. She was an excellent systems engineer—reliable, precise, dedicated to systems thinking and design thinking principles. Nevertheless, her tense demeanor, constantly searching eyes, and perpetually anxious manner irritated Lawrence.

"Come in, Hernández," he said.

Hernández pushed her way inside, standing there in her dripping rain gear, blinking against the overhead lights.

Lawrence closed the door and nodded toward Lambert's bent form with a slight smile. "Our architectural consultant is hard at work on her latest design—the Ashford Harbor renovation project."

Hernández had no answering smile, although there had been considerable good-natured discussion aboard the Meridian ever since the Navy Department had assigned the architect to the vessel to continue her work during the convoy.

"I'm concerned, sir," Hernández said. "I'm not confident about the autonomous navigation readings. This storm—"

Lawrence put a reassuring hand on Hernández's shoulder. "Relax! Don't let a minor discrepancy worry you."

"But this storm, sir!" Hernández pulled away from his touch, avoiding his eyes. "It's affecting the sensor arrays. Variable electromagnetic interference. Choppy readings from the seafloor mapping—as if there are uncharted currents among these coastal formations. No way to verify by satellite, and now—look at this!"

She held out the tablet. The data streams were fluctuating wildly.

"You said there might be a way to verify?" Lawrence asked. "Clear satellite window?"

"Just briefly, sir, and I'm wondering—" Her voice trailed off, but her eyes moved toward the backup navigation console.

Lieutenant Commander Lawrence shrugged good-naturedly and moved to the console. "Not that I doubt your readings, Ava, but since you asked."

Lawrence accessed the satellite link and ran a manual verification. In a few minutes he returned and handed Hernández a printout with coordinates marked clearly.

"Here's what the satellite confirms," the commander told his systems engineer. "I bet your autonomous readings aren't far off."

Hernández stared at the data, then slowly held up her own tablet display.

Lawrence frowned, grabbed his printout again. "Any time my manual check differs this much from your autonomous systems reading, we're stopping to investigate," he declared, comparing the two sets of coordinates and quickly rechecking his figures. "We're still in Selvorian waters—a long way from where we need to be."

"Signal the convoy to halt," he told Hernández. "We can't afford to proceed in these waters with this level of navigation uncertainty."

Hernández complied, and the subtle vibration of the Meridian's propulsion systems decreased immediately. Hernández said: "I've been thinking, sir, whether we should try to get a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons. With all these rocks and shallow areas—"

"Radio?" interrupted Dr. Lambert, inserting herself between them in her independent way that ignored military protocol. "You're using radio navigation?" She broke into a knowing chuckle, her keen eyes twinkling behind wire-rimmed glasses. "Go ahead and try it. See what response you get! It will be no better than what enemy forces would get when Jennifer Lambert implements her communication disruption protocols! Try it! Try it, I say!"

Mateo Lawrence stared at her, questioning her mental state. Then he hurried to the communications center, with Hernández close behind, and Lambert following.

The door opened as they approached it. A worried communications officer emerged, still wearing his headset, staring up at the antenna array with confusion.

"Get us a radio triangulation from the coastal beacons immediately," Lawrence said sharply, noting the officer's distracted state.

"Triangulation, sir?" The man brought his eyes down reluctantly, still troubled. "I'm sorry, sir, but the system's dead. Went offline about five minutes ago. I was monitoring weather updates when everything cut out. I was checking for hardware failures."

Lambert giggled. Lawrence gave her another concerned look and entered the communications center.

"Try again!" he told the officer. "See what you can raise!"

The communications officer returned to his station and worked frantically. Again and again, he sent requests for triangulation from the coastal beacon network that had recently been established to ensure safe passage for autonomous convoys, but there was no response on any frequency—not even commercial traffic on the standard bands, nor chatter from other vessels on the emergency channels.

"Dead!" Lambert muttered, with a bitter laugh. "Yet not dead, gentlemen! The equipment is undamaged. The signals themselves have been disrupted. I have created an interference field around your vessel, just as I can eventually create them throughout enemy-controlled waters! For the next two hours, no radio communications can enter or leave my zone of disruption—my field of refracted electromagnetic waves, generated by my experimental station on one of the nearby islands!"

There was a long pause as commander and engineer stared at her.

Lawrence was the first to speak.

"Your secrecy could cost the United States Navy an entire convoy—and us our lives!" he said angrily. "We need that triangulation now! If you're not delusional, shut down your system until we determine our exact position!"

Lambert spread her hands helplessly. "I cannot. I have programmed my automated assistant system to maintain two hours of communication disruption! I cannot send a message to override it, because our radio is dead!"

As if to mock her, the ship's radio suddenly activated:

"Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian. Beacon Station Alpha-7 calling convoy leader Meridian—"

"Convoy leader Meridian responding to Beacon Alpha-7!" the officer intoned, exchanging glances with the two officers over Lambert's embarrassment, and requested position data.

The answer came back: "Position bearing northeast by quarter east, convoy leader Meridian!"

Lawrence sighed with relief. He noticed that Hernández was staring intently at the communications officer as he continued: "Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4. Convoy leader Meridian calling Beacon Station Beta-4—"

Then the system crackled again: "Beacon Station Beta-4 responding to convoy leader Meridian. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west. Position bearing northwest by three degrees west, convoy leader Meridian."

Commander and engineer had both recorded the coordinates. Ignoring Lambert's protests that signals had somehow penetrated her disruption field, they rushed to the navigation center.

Quickly they plotted the bearings from the designated points. Clean intersecting lines confirmed their position.

Lawrence frowned and shook his head. Slowly he managed a reluctant grin as he extended his hand.

"Good work, Ava," he said. "Looks like you and the radio triangulation are correct. Resume course as planned."

"I'm relieved, sir, all the same," Hernández admitted, "to have the radio confirmation. We would have run aground if you'd been right."

They continued through the night. The brief clear patch in the clouds had closed. The sky was again a solid mass of darkness pouring sheets of rain.

Hernández returned to her station, and Lambert went back to the commander's workspace. Lawrence lingered in the communications center with the officer.

"Strange thing," the officer said, still working the controls and frowning, "how I got that triangulation through and now can't raise anything else. I'm wondering if that architect really has done something to the electromagnetic spectrum. The equipment seems fine."

He continued checking the systems, testing and retesting. Indicators showed normal; connections were live and sent familiar tingles through his testing fingers.

Lawrence left him and went to rejoin Lambert. He found the architect pacing, gesturing in the air, pausing periodically to run her fingers through her silver hair or tug nervously at her collar.

"You have witnessed a demonstration, commander!" she declared. "My demonstration! My technology has disrupted electromagnetic communications in this area completely."

"Seems to me," Lawrence said dryly, "this technology could harm friendly forces as much as enemies."

The architect drew herself to her full height—barely five feet four. Her voice grew sharp. "Wait! Just wait! There are complementary technologies to work with this one. Combined properly, they will counter the autonomous warfare systems that have devastated the regions where I've worked!"

Lawrence was somewhat disturbed by the intensity in Lambert's eyes behind her glasses. There was something fierce in the woman's expression, as her jaw clenched.

"Those containers you have in the cargo bay," Lawrence said, "are they connected to this communication disruption?"

A distant look came into Lambert's eyes. She seemed not to hear the question. She lowered her voice: "My sister is still in Riverside, Xandria. So are my nieces, and my brother and his family. If hostile forces knew what I'm developing, all of them would be in danger. You understand—in grave danger?"

Lawrence said: "I understand."

"And if enemy agents in Selvoria knew of the island from which my disruption field is projected—" Lambert paused, her head tilting, as if listening—

On deck, there was shouting and commotion. Lawrence rushed out, grabbing his rain gear as he went. The alert from the forward watch had been relayed across the ship. The words struck Lawrence's ears with ominous weight.

"Shallow water ahead!"

He reached Hernández at the main control station and saw the helmsman working the manual override controls, trying to bring the autonomous steering hard to port.

Then the ship struck. Everything loose flew forward until it hit the end of its restraints or crashed into something solid.

Lawrence felt Hernández's hand grip his arm as she leaned close and shouted: "You must have been right, sir, and the radio triangulation and my autonomous readings wrong. We've hit that reef hard. I'm afraid we're breached!"

"Deploy the emergency seals!" Lawrence ordered. "We should be able to keep her afloat!"

And then he became aware of a profound stillness. A vast wall of silence enveloped the entire vessel. Looking over the side, he could no longer see the waves that moments before had beaten against the hull.

The Meridian was shrouded in a massive cloud of yellowish-gray vapor, and more was rising from below—from ventilation systems and access hatches and observation ports—as if the entire ship were flooding with some toxic gas.

Lawrence's mind flashed to stories he'd heard of military installations during recent conflicts that had fallen when defenders found themselves struck unconscious by gas that had been introduced into their facilities' ventilation systems.

There were theories about infiltrators who had compromised the systems, while others attributed the gas deployment to insider saboteurs. There were dozens of explanations—

The vapor clouds enveloping the Meridian were thickening. All around the deck lay the forms of unconscious crew members, suddenly stricken helpless. And then Lawrence saw other forms moving through the deck—forms that looked otherworldly, but he recognized them for what they were—people wearing gas masks.

Hernández was nowhere visible. The helmsman lay unconscious beside the drifting controls. Then a gas-masked figure appeared through the vapor and steadied the helm, preventing the vessel from being completely at the mercy of wind and waves.

Lawrence heard the anchor deploy, as if by invisible hands, the chain screaming and clanking through the mechanism. Then he was completely surrounded by the yellowish-gray mist. He felt his consciousness fading.

Voices murmured all around him in confused conversation—accented voices that rose and fell in excited discussion. He caught occasional English words mixed with what sounded like Eastern European phonetics.

Two phrases registered clearly in his mind. One was "Prometheus cargo"; the other was "supply chain." But gradually his hearing began to fade, as if someone were placing cotton in his ears. He couldn't breathe properly; a fog seemed to be rising within him until it overwhelmed his thoughts—

He felt something strike his head and realized he had collapsed on the deck. And after that, he was aware of nothing—

The rain had diminished to a light mist. The gentle motion of the surf rocked the Meridian in a lazy, rolling rhythm as she lay with her bow pressed into the sandbar at the inlet entrance.

From the bridge, Systems Engineer Ava Hernández watched the gas-masked figures moving about the decks, descending into compartments—like phantoms from a nightmare. Hernández looked phantom-like herself, her face covered by a respirator. Beside her stood her co-conspirator Robert Valdez, also wearing a gas mask.

Hernández spoke quietly, her lips near Valdez's ear. "It worked, Robert."

"Yeah," Valdez agreed. "Worked perfectly."

The unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew were being carried to the lowered boarding platform and transferred into waiting boats.

Hernández cursed under her breath. "Estimate it'll take a few hours before the ship's clear of that gas."

Valdez shook his head. "The architect says she's got a neutralizing agent in one of those containers that'll clear everything in thirty minutes."

"I'd prefer to operate without Lambert if possible," Hernández muttered. "She's unstable."

"It was an unstable genius who invented the disruption technology that broke the autonomous defense networks in the Xandrian conflict," Valdez reminded her. "It saved countless resources—resources that would have been lost if the facilities had to be taken by direct assault."

Hernández grunted and turned away. A compact figure in the uniform of a foreign naval officer had climbed the boarding platform and was ascending to the bridge. She too wore a respirator.

She approached Hernández, saluted, and extended her hand, introducing herself as Commander Li Munoz. She began speaking in Mandarin, but Hernández stopped her.

"I don't speak Mandarin," she explained. "I was born and raised in the United States—by parents who had suffered economic inequality in the previous generation. My mother died when our family lost everything. My father—" She paused and cleared her throat.

"Yes? Your father?" the foreign officer prompted, switching to accented English.

"My father dedicated me to a mission of correction—to address the wrongs done to our family," Hernández continued. "If America's economic system hadn't failed my family, he wouldn't have lost his livelihood; my mother would still be alive. When he joined the resistance movement, the path became clear to use me—to educate me in military academy, then place me in the United States Navy for a career—and no one suspected me. No one—"

"Sometimes," Valdez interjected, "I thought Lawrence suspected you."

"Perhaps Lawrence will discover his suspicions were justified," Hernández said bitterly. "But it won't help Lawrence—a commander who's lost his convoy." She turned to Munoz. "You have sufficient personnel to operate the Meridian?"

Munoz nodded. "We have a complete crew—one hundred and fifty people—officers, engineers, technicians, communications specialists, all trained operatives who have been positioned here secretly over the past two months."

The three—Munoz, Hernández and Valdez—stood on the bridge and talked while the efficient teams worked systematically to remove the unconscious bodies of the Meridian's crew and transport them to shore.

And when that task was completed, boats began arriving alongside with sophisticated equipment, additional gas containers like those Lambert had brought aboard, and power systems and batteries that looked like something from a technological nightmare.

And supervising everything, shouting commands in multiple languages, gesturing emphatically to clarify her directions, was the energetic figure of Dr. Jennifer Lambert!

"The architect's in her element," Hernández remarked to Commander Munoz.

"Interesting about her," Valdez added, "is that her designs actually function. That disruption field isolated us completely."

Commander Munoz nodded. "Good. But you transmitted your position data—the false coordinates?"

"Yes," Hernández said. "That came through as planned. And Lawrence will have considerable difficulty explaining it."

"From now on," Munoz said seriously, "the disruption field will be projected from the Meridian, and we have another of Lambert's technologies that will be even more valuable when we intercept the Prometheus from its convoy."

"The Prometheus?" Hernández asked, puzzled.

Munoz said: "She's a cargo vessel in a convoy departing Juniper, Relvaria—fifteen thousand tons. The orders are to capture her intact, not sink her."

"What's the objective?"

"Her cargo," Munoz explained. "It's more valuable than gold. It includes a major shipment of rare earth elements."

"Rare earths?" Hernández repeated. "What's special about them?"

"Rare earth elements," Munoz told her, "are critical minerals—necessary for advanced electronics and autonomous systems, far more valuable to us than precious metals. They're essential for manufacturing advanced technology. They come from restricted sources—and our supply is critically low."

"I would think we could obtain these rare earths directly through established channels," Hernández said, "without the risk of capturing a United States Navy convoy vessel."

"There are other materials desperately needed aboard the Prometheus," Munoz explained. "Advanced semiconductors and specialized alloys and hundreds of containers of precision components for autonomous systems. Our intelligence has been monitoring the convoys for months for exactly this type of cargo that the Prometheus is transporting."

"Can we trust Lambert?" Hernández asked, with sudden suspicion.

"Yes," Munoz assured her. "Of all people—we can trust Lambert."

"But she's American," Hernández argued.

"Our organization manages Americans and Europeans and others whom it recruits as operatives," Munoz pointed out. "Lambert has a sister and other relatives in Riverside. She knows that if anything fails, if there's the slightest indication of betrayal on her part, her sister and the others will suffer. Lambert's loyalty is guaranteed."

Hernández turned to observe the forward section of the Meridian. The masked foreign crew members were installing some apparatus there—a strange device that resembled an advanced sensor array, connected by cables to the room that served as Lambert's design studio and laboratory.

Another team was installing communications equipment in the aft superstructure.

Descending to check the lower decks, Hernández found that ventilation ports were being opened and crews were dispersing chemicals to clear the atmosphere of the gas that had overcome the Meridian's American crew.

Returning to the bridge, she found that the tide in the inlet had risen significantly, and the vessel was floating more freely at anchor.

Then, at Munoz's orders, the anchor was raised, and boats and a powered launch were used to help maneuver the vessel completely free of the sandbar. This was accomplished smoothly.

Munoz approached where Hernández was standing on the bridge and extended her hand.

"Congratulations, Commander Hernández!" she said. "We have captured one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels!" She made a gesture as if raising a glass in toast. "To success!" she added.

"To success!" Hernández repeated, and the two smiled at each other.

Stars were visible in a patch of dark sky, and broken masses of gray cloud were racing before the wind. Lieutenant Commander Mateo Lawrence found himself lying in wet sand on a beach somewhere, with the rain—now a light drizzle—falling on his face. He was cold; his limbs were stiff and numb. His nose and throat felt scorched inside, as if a wave of searing heat had burned them.

According to his last calculations, the Meridian had been leading a convoy along the Selvorian coast, still days away from reaching Wendrian waters. This probably was one of the islands in that region, or possibly the mainland.

It was difficult getting to his feet, and when he managed to stand, he could only plant his feet in the sand and sway unsteadily for a full minute, like someone learning to walk again.

All around him in the near-total darkness, he could make out dim forms of people sprawled on the beach, and others moving about, exploring. He heard murmuring voices and saw the glow of flashlights.

Someone with a flashlight was approaching. Its white beam shone briefly in Lawrence's face, and the familiar voice of Junior Officer Raj Price spoke: "Commander Lawrence! Are you all right, sir?"

"I think so." Lawrence's heart warmed at the concerned expression on Price's face, the genuine worry in his dark eyes. The young officer was earnest, dedicated, thoroughly sincere in his emotions. "How about you, Raj?" Lawrence added.

"Headache from the gas, but nothing serious. Any orders, sir?"

Lawrence thought for a moment. "Assemble the crew as best you can. We'll attempt a roll call. Any sign of the ship?"

There was a somber note in Price's voice. "No, sir. She's been freed from the sandbar and taken to sea."

The words hit Lawrence with the numbing shock of a physical blow. For the first time, he fully grasped the catastrophe that had befallen him. He had lost his ship—one of the United States Navy's most advanced autonomous convoy vessels—under circumstances that strongly suggested treachery and sabotage.

As he reflected, he realized he might have prevented the loss if he had been more alert, more suspicious. For it was clear now that the Meridian had been deliberately guided to this location; that those who had seized her had been waiting here for precisely that purpose.

The pieces fit together like a puzzle—Lambert's disruption field; the radio coordinates; Systems Engineer Hernández's suspicious behavior. They were all part of a carefully orchestrated plan.

All the questionable circumstances surrounding Hernández flooded into Lawrence's mind. He had never fully trusted her; never felt comfortable with her. Hernández always acted as if she harbored secrets.

Lawrence recalled that Hernández and Lambert had held long private discussions—conversations they would abruptly end when anyone else approached. And Hernández had always been close to the most problematic crew member—Robert Valdez.

Lawrence moved around, locating the officers, issuing orders. There were still some unconscious personnel to be revived. In a sheltered area among the rocks, an exploring group had found enough dry driftwood to build a fire—

In another hour, the skies had cleared, and bright moonlight flooded the scene with ghostly illumination. The crew of the Meridian had all regained consciousness and were drying themselves around the large driftwood fires in the cove.

Lawrence ordered a signal beacon maintained on a high point. Then he organized the crew, according to their departments, for a check of the missing.

When this was completed, it was determined that the Meridian's entire complement of one hundred and ten personnel were present—except Systems Engineer Ava Hernández and crew member Robert Valdez! And Dr. Jennifer Lambert was also missing!

With dawn's arrival, brief exploration revealed that the Meridian's crew was stranded on an island, roughly one square mile in area; that they had been put ashore without food or additional clothing or equipment of any kind, and that no boats had been left for them.

One search party reported finding the remnants of what had been a communications station on a high point on the north shore of the island. Another had found the remains of temporary structures, recently dismantled, in a small, wooded depression—a well-concealed location invisible from the air unless flying very low; a place where one hundred and fifty or more people could have camped.

There was adequate water—a small stream fed by springs—but no food. Evidently food was a valuable resource the recent inhabitants couldn't afford to leave behind.

Lawrence was examining the wreckage of the communications station, wondering if this might have been the source of Lambert's disruption field, when Junior Officer Raj Price approached him.

"There's a coast guard vessel heading for the island, sir," he announced.

Lawrence nodded grimly, already composing in his mind how he would explain this disaster—and how he would begin the hunt for those who had betrayed them.

"Send up another signal flare," Lawrence ordered. "The Navy will want a full accounting of what happened."

Price hesitated, his young face troubled. "Sir, do you think we'll face an inquiry? About the loss of the cargo?"

Lawrence's jaw tightened. He thought of the manifest he'd reviewed before departure—the specialized construction equipment, the prefabricated structural components, the industrial materials that Lambert had personally requested be included in the shipment. "There will certainly be questions about why none of it reached its intended recipient."

"And Dr. Lambert's designs?" Price asked. "She was supposed to oversee the installation personally, wasn't she?"

"The Navy made arrangements for her to continue working during transit," Lawrence said bitterly. "It seemed efficient at the time—she could finalize her architectural plans while we transported the materials she'd need." He laughed, a harsh sound. "Now I understand why she was so insistent on joining this particular convoy."

Price nodded slowly. "The harbormaster in Ashford will be wondering what happened to his shipment. That port expansion was supposed to begin next month."

"Ashford will have to wait," Lawrence said. "Along with everyone else in Wendria who was counting on this cargo."

Price moved off to signal the approaching vessel. Lawrence stood alone on the rocky outcrop, watching the coast guard ship grow larger on the horizon. He thought about the voyage that should have continued westward through Selvorian waters and across the strait—about the port city where Lambert's blueprints were supposed to become reality, where the cargo holds full of construction equipment would have been unloaded at modern docking facilities.

Instead, the Meridian was gone, her cargo stolen, and Lawrence was stranded here with nothing but questions and the bitter knowledge that he had been outmaneuvered from the moment Lambert stepped aboard in Bridgewater.

The coast guard vessel drew closer. Soon he would have to explain how a routine supply run had ended in catastrophe, how the convoy never completed its crossing to Wendrian waters, and how an American architect had orchestrated the theft of a United States Navy vessel. The inquiry would be long and unpleasant.

But first, Lawrence vowed, he would see Hernández and Lambert brought to justice—wherever they had taken his ship.
